review:
Story
        The concept of an adult hitman trapped in a kid's body isn't a crazy new idea, but it still feels relatively fresh here and has some genuinely good moments. That being said, for a show with a comedy tag, the humor is incredibly low-effort and repetitive. I was honestly confused by how many "jokes" there were about women's equal rights and gender roles. We get a reminder every five minutes that "women can do XYZ too." At some point, you have to ask: why is this a running gag? The MC is a 39-year-old from the modern era, not some time-traveler reincarnated from the 19th century. The show spams this exact same "joke" so much that I had to check if I was watching a Netflix production or if the author just couldn't think of any other punchlines. Aside from that weird fixation, the rest of the story is actually fine.

        Visuals
        Going by the premise, you might expect your typical low-budget "seasonal slop," but the production quality is actually a pleasant surprise. The animation is solid, and there is a good amount of detail and varied scene composition. It isn't a breathtaking masterpiece, but it is surprisingly well-made and definitely above average for this type of show.

        Conclusion
        Is it worth watching? Because it leans so heavily into being a comedy, we probably aren't going to get any serious or deep plot development. The fact that the show is already reusing the exact same lazy joke ten times in just three episodes makes me worry that the humor has already run dry. However, if you can look past the repetitive gags, it still might turn out to be a decent watch.

review:
In a cringe industry the cringe assassin setting reigns supreme. While I remember how exciting it was to watch shounen as a kid, at my current age I struggle to force down any action centric manga, not to mention the absolute edgelord cringebeast of a subgenre assassins tends to lend to.
    The reason that Kill Blue isn’t automatically trash like the rest of the subgenre, is the same reason "Yakuza-psychich" isn’t trash. They actually explore the consequences of a body swap. I find it utterly asinine that with so much reincarnation/body swapping tropes flying around, the discontinuities between the different lives of the reincarnator and the host are never REALLY explored. Suddenly the plot wand is waved and the author has permanently moved on to things he really cares about like his shameless self insertion fetish.
    Here as well, The Old man of the Mountain’s legendary occupation is done dirty by unrealistic and cringey personalities and tropes, enough to possibly spur an actual hired killer to want to kill himself if he had to sit through it. Personally, I tend to skip most fighting scenes anyway so it’s not much of an issue.
    What made this all palatable however, was how our MC Oogami kept being an old man on the inside, and based his outlook and relations as such. I feel emotional maturity from an author who writes our MC as an old rugged man in a boy's body attempting to reciprocate friendship and affection from his mentally younger peers in an adequate fashion.
    I enjoy a story with an unrealistic setting, where the author attempts to make every interaction realistic. Compared to a story where body swap dynamics are realistically portrayed, such as The Beginning before the end, it doesn’t get close. But as the saying goes in Spanish, "algo es algo, dijo un calvo".

There were some episodes that did GREAT things with the lore (spoiler alert: A2's "origin" and those promising glimpses of Replicant) and THAT IS what this show should've been: a COMPLEMENT to its source material, NOT an intent to tell its story in a WAY shorter and less complex form of media. Art and animation are average at best, with a couple moments of brilliancy, but too many of mediocrity (also, those gratuitous butt-shots of 2B are cringy to say the least). The OP song by Aimer is horrendous (and I love Aimer), but at least Amazarashi's ED one doesn't feel that off. Not a negative word for the rest of the OST, though (and voice acting), as it's taken straight from the video game... but sadly misused more than once. In short: this show could've been REALLY "something" if CHANGES were for the sake of a new experience and not for an "easy way out" (and if its overall quality was WAY better). As it is, I can't honestly recommend "Ver1.1a". Want "NieR"? Play the games. That, you won't ever regret.

Go For It, Nakamura-kun!! is an anime about what it's like to be fifteen and turn stupid around your crush. That is to say, it's an anime I have to pause every five minutes to recover from secondhand embarrassment before I can continue watching.

I am aware that this is entirely subjective. Some people find cringe comedy funny. Furthermore, it's probably less embarrassing if you find it relatable, and my high school years were absent of many of the typical teenage experiences, such as having crushes. In fact, it's even harder for me to buy into this show on account of the fact I've never understood crushing on someone you barely know. I am fully willing to admit I'm probably not the target audience, especially considering I don't find Watamote embarrassing on account of the fact I have social anxiety disorder and it feels more like teasing my younger self. So I'm sure former teenage hopeless romantics find this relatable and funny.

However, this review is my opinion. Nothing is truly objective. And in my opinion this is truly an uncomfortable watch.

Now, there are still things I like about it. I love the 80s-esque art. I think the characters are charming (except Hirose, who ironically feels a bit shallow). It does have funny jokes at times.

But man. I don't know how many more episodes of this I can handle.

review:
Death Note, it's been 20 years since the anime was made. As always with popular anime, I wasn't interested in watching it at first, but since I was running out of manga to read, I reached for this work. The manga surprised me in the end and after reading it I quite liked it, which unfortunately I can't say about the anime. I quickly went through the reviews here on MAL and apparently everyone only knows the anime, which is why they praise it to the heavens as a masterpiece.

I'm disappointed with the anime, since I dare say that up to 30% of the overall plot from the manga is simply omitted or changed. The manga has a huge amount of both dialogues and monologues and MADHOUSE cut most of them out and it's no wonder when the ep. are less than 23 min long. so it's understandable that everything won't fit in there. Another thing I didn't like was the anime canon/manga ep. although there weren't many of them (ep. 1,25-26,37), but overall it spoils the key moments in the plot. I will also agree that the second half is actually unnecessary, since light is just putting on a show, catching kira. That part is less interesting and I felt the same way about the manga, but it was interesting what the author would come up with to keep the plot from ending. The drawing/animation didn't interest me that much, to be disappointed, but the OST surprised me and I heard a few songs there that I wouldn't even guess came from DN, such as the L theme, the OP/ED didn't blow me away.

So for me, the anime is a big disappointment, despite the fact that it had a "proper" ending. Personally, I strongly recommend reading the manga first. If I hadn't read it, I would have definitely reacted the same way as everyone else and I thought that since it has such high ratings, they made a point of it.

review:
This anime can be best described as the the "I Love Science" meme in animated form

The "Pop-Philosophy" Problem
On the surface, Orb: On the Movements of the Earth presents itself as a gritty, intellectual exploration of the heliocentric revolution. However, for anyone who has actually read Ockham, Aquinas, or even basic commentaries on the Ptolemaic system, the experience is akin to watching a "Science vs. Religion" YouTube video from 2011. It is the quintessential "Reddit-esque" anime: it prioritizes the feeling of being enlightened over the actual substance of the philosophy it name-drops. It is right up the alley of those dorks that call themselves historians but their only interest is WW2 and they skimmed a few wikipedia articles. That group shares a fan base with this one.

Story: A Surface-Level Caricature
The core issue is that the show views history through a modern lens, stripping away the actual intellectual tension of the era. The transition from geocentrism to heliocentrism wasn't a battle between "rational heroes" and "evil dogmatic villains"; it was a complex mathematical and observational struggle. There is no actual depth to what was going on in the day to day life surrounding this subject.
Not to mention the Orb, "truth" is treated like a magical spark that instantly makes characters superior to their peers. The show ignores the fact that, at the time, the Ptolemaic model was actually a highly functional, mathematically elegant system that accounted for most observable data better than early heliocentric models did. By ignoring the genuine logic of the geocentric worldview, the show loses its stakes.

Characters: Archetypes Over People
The characters don't feel like people of their time; they feel like modern secularists wearing 15th-century costumes. They speak in grand, sweeping aphorisms about "The Truth" and "Reason" that feel incredibly anachronistic. Pretty much every character is some form of trope especially "I must know the truth at any cost" trope.
The Inquisitors = Effectively cartoon villains who represent "The System."

The use of William of Ockham’s principles is particularly grating. Rather than engaging with the nuance of parsimony in medieval logic, the show uses "Ockham’s Razor" as a buzzword—a "gotcha" tool that the protagonist wields like a superpower. It’s surface-level name-dropping designed to make the audience feel smart for recognizing the term, without actually demanding they understand its application.
Why was nominalism even brought up in the show? They didnt discuss anything at all about it. Its literally just constant name dropping so rick and morty dorks found their next holy grail of a tv show calling them the smartest guy in the room.

Presentation: SO FUCKING BORING
The pacing is sluggish, often stalling for long, repetitive monologues about the beauty of the universe that say very little of substance.

Art & Sound
The production values are competent but fail to elevate the material. The character designs are somewhat unique, but the direction often feels static, relying on "talking heads" and extreme close-ups to carry the emotional weight that the script fails to provide.

Conclusion
I have to say that only a specific subset of people like this kind of show. And it certainly deserves points off for being so uninteresting that even the ""dude space!"" potheads would find this a complete snorefest. So what we are left with is astronomy nerds who got wedgies in middle school. The End

review:
One Punch Man Season 3 is not just a continuation of the series — it is a statement. A bold, genre-breaking triumph that somehow manages to parody shōnen anime while simultaneously becoming the best shōnen anime ever made.

From the very first episode, it’s clear: this season came to end careers.

Animation: A Visual Flex

Season 3 delivers animation so fluid it feels illegal. Every punch lands with the weight of a collapsing star. Fight choreography is cinematic, inventive, and absurdly detailed — proving once and for all that whoever animated this season hated their wrists but loved their art.

Garou’s fights alone deserve their own museum exhibit. The camera work, the lighting, the sheer brutality — it’s not animation anymore, it’s violence poetry.

Storytelling: Satire Meets Substance

What makes Season 3 a masterpiece is how it balances stupidity and philosophy.

Yes, Saitama still ends fights with one punch.
Yes, it’s still hilarious.

But beneath the comedy lies a surprisingly deep exploration of:

What it means to be a hero

The loneliness of absolute strength

Society’s obsession with labels and rankings

Garou’s arc is handled with such emotional nuance that you almost forget he’s fighting people who can throw buildings. Almost.

Characters: Everyone Gets Their Moment

This season does the impossible: every character matters.

Saitama remains effortlessly hilarious while quietly tragic

Genos evolves from a punchline into a genuinely moving character

Side heroes who were once jokes now feel legendary

Even background characters show more development than protagonists in other anime

By the end, you care about people you couldn’t even name in Season 1.

Humor: Perfectly Timed Chaos

The comedy is sharper than ever. Jokes land in the middle of life-or-death battles. Dramatic monologues are obliterated by Saitama’s boredom. The contrast between cosmic stakes and mundane reactions is peak One Punch Man.

You’ll laugh. Then immediately question existence. Then laugh again.

Sound & Music: Goosebumps Guaranteed

The soundtrack is relentless. Hero themes hit like war drums. Villain motifs feel operatic. Silence is used so well that sometimes the lack of music is the most powerful moment of all.

The opening? Instant classic. The ending? Emotionally unfair.

Final Verdict

One Punch Man Season 3 achieves what most anime never dare attempt:

It respects its roots

Expands its world

Deepens its themes

And still remembers that it’s supposed to be fun

It’s satire perfected. Action elevated. Comedy weaponized.

Final Score: 10/10
Not just anime of the year — anime of the decade.

If this season doesn’t win awards that don’t even exist yet, then awards are meaningless.

review:
Honestly, I had high expectations for this title, as the Fate franchise includes several very good anime entries. Unfortunately, both the technical execution and the storytelling in this work fall well short of those expectations. The animation overall feels underdeveloped: movements are often choppy, character faces are missing or only partially rendered, and still frames are used repeatedly. The audio quality is also unconvincing. Lip syncing is inconsistent, with dialogue frequently not properly matched to mouth movements, which further weakens the overall presentation.

In terms of content, the story closely follows the familiar Fate series formula centered around the Holy Grail War. While there are minor deviations, such as changes to the rules or the setting, these offer little in the way of fresh ideas. Additionally, both the narrative structure and many of the summoned servants are already familiar from previous installments, giving the work little sense of individuality.

Conclusion: Fate/strange Fake: Whispers of Dawn serves as an introduction to the recently released anime. However, since its animation, style, and shortcomings are nearly identical to those of the film, this prologue offers little added value. For this reason, I see no reason to continue with the full anime adaptation.

review:
For many years I thought Oregairu Kan was the worse romcom I’d ever seen, but I can now confidently say Watari-kun surpassed it. For 6 months I subjected myself to the torture of watching these episodes. Why? Well, I’ve never dropped anything and refused to let this garbage break that streak, no matter how much it infuriated me. Plus, you can’t make an informed and educated review on something if you haven’t seen it all. While it does improve slightly at the end, the characters in this show are all so frustratingly dumb and the story so poorly written, it’s not worth sticking around. I only sat through this because of my inability to drop shows and wishing, hoping, PRAYING that Ishihara got the happy ending she deserved. The average person doesn’t have the time to subject themselves to things they don’t like, so I’d highly recommend avoiding this show.

I’m not going to waste time giving this some flowery and well thought out critical analysis like I usually do with my reviews. This show is too bad for that. I’ll get right to the point. Why do I hate this show? Simple, the MC is a spineless coward and a pushover, the female lead who wins is predictable from the start(first volume cover gimmick) is so unlikeable she makes me want to vomit every time she’s on screen. They’re childhood friends and she’s cute so that totally justifies her stalking the MC and sabotaging his love life with the girl he’s had a crush on for years, right? According to Satsuki’s fervent and extremely loyal fanbase, yes. For me, this was so cringe and immediately got this show off on a bad foot. Satsuki constantly comes between Ishihara and Naoto and does everything in her power to make Ishihara, who already has issues due to past trauma, even more insecure. Yes, trying to seduce a guy you know has a girlfriend is wrong. Again, this gets brushed off because she’s attractive and the author tries giving her some sob story to make us empathize with her, I’m not buying it though. She’s a POS and even though we all knew the ending was going to be what it was, it doesn’t make me any less annoyed that it turned out the way it did. "Ishihara isn’t perfect either bro, stop putting her on a pedestal" yes, I’m quite aware that Ishihara is a flawed character who needed to work through a lot of issues in this series before getting in a relationship, however that does not negate anything I said about Satsuki. She still exasperated things and put Ishihara in some really difficult situations that didn’t need to happen if she just respected boundaries.

Speaking of boundaries, don’t even get me started on the whole possessive thing the MC and his sister had going on for most of the series. Now again, they explain this with some backstory about their parents and you’re supposed to empathize with Suzu, but empathizing≠liking or thinking something’s ok. This is still a very unhealthy and toxic dynamic that’s uncomfortable to watch for probably the first cour of the show. Thankfully, it gets better and Suzu does arguably have the best character development in the entire series, but for a while there, it was sketchy. The concept of boundaries is really important in the series overall, though as we see Satsuki struggle with them, Ishihara, Touki, the Kouhai love interest.. etc. Everyone in this show needed a nice therapy session for unpack all the trauma they went through. I get what the author was trying to do in making a broken, flawed cast especially since it’s a seinen story, but the problem is it’s just not good. Can anyone really look at this series and say Naoto was a good protagonist? Will he be remembered? No. If you liked this show, you found Satsuki attractive and wanted her to be happy, the MC, even with his growth in the last few episodes, is just utterly boring and uninspired. You know it’s a wish fulfilment story because none of these girls should’ve fallen for him.

Story’s weak, but the production values are just as bad. This show looks like a slideshow for most of its run and the few good episodes it has aren’t much better. The voice acting is decent, character designs are OK, but it’s a bad anime in production and writing.

I sat through this garbage so you don’t have to. I don’t regret it because I did like seeing those moments where Ishihara was happy and I liked a couple of the supporting characters, but this was just such a bad watch. I hate the main couple as individuals and as a couple, everyone acts like an idiot, drama for the sake of drama.. this felt like a shitty afternoon soap opera with none of the charm.

Watari-kun gets a very easy 1 out of 10.

review:
Story
Both the romance and the overarching plot are mediocre at best. Let's start with the obvious: many of us were completely baited by the first 30 seconds of the anime. With a 17+ rating and a brutal opening scene, it promised a much darker, heavier show than your typical seasonal anime. Yet, outside of that very first scene, there is barely anything mature or intense about it, which is a massive disappointment.

Furthermore, the world-building is incredibly shallow. If your country's ultimate secret weapon is a 10-year-old girl and you are forced to send orphaned kids to the front lines, your nation is losing the war terribly. The fact that there is zero pushback, political tension, or realism regarding this desperate situation just exposes how poorly thought-out the plot actually is. On top of that, the way the anime over-romanticizes and over-sexualizes these young characters is highly off-putting. It feels like a very cheap trick used to mask a badly written romance.

Visuals
The visual aspect of this anime is the complete opposite of its storytelling. The animation, background scenery, attention to detail, and visual effects are all exceptionally well done. It is a genuinely gorgeous show to look at, which honestly just makes the narrative failures feel like even more of a waste.

Conclusion
Is it worth watching? No. This is a cheap romance story that feels like it could have been generated by an AI five years ago. Yes, the visuals are fantastic, but a pretty coat of paint isn't enough to save a shallow, illogical plot. Visuals aren't everything, and for that reason, I absolutely cannot recommend this.

There is absolutely no moral gray area here. The storytelling feels incredibly childish, strongly reminding me of children's books where the good guys always win, the bad guys always lose, and there is no deeper thought or nuance required. That simplistic logic might work for a kids' book, but for a full-fledged anime, it just leaves the plot feeling completely flat.

Visuals
The visual production is mediocre at best. There is absolutely nothing special or memorable about the art direction, the character designs, or the animation, to be honest.

Conclusion
Is it worth watching? If you are looking for a safe, simplistic anime to watch with a young child, this might actually be a decent choice. However, for a standard anime viewer, the world-building and narrative are just way too shallow and uninteresting to be worth your time.
